passage: Gurleen, you are fuming about the drilling upstairs, so listen. When I was twenty-five I lived beneath a man who rehearsed tabla at night. For three weeks I lay awake composing speeches. One night I stood in the stairwell, fists clenched, and thought: if I knock now, I will say something ugly. I went back inside. The next Sunday I knocked with a plate of pakoras and said, "I love the music, but after ten I hear every beat through the ceiling. Could you play before nine, or put a mat under the drum?" He blinked, then laughed, and slid a folded blanket under it that same evening. If he had not, I had the society rules to fall back on. I never needed them. Talk first, Gurleen. Kishore

qa.q: What did Kishore bring when knocking on the neighbour's door?
qa.a: Kishore brought a plate of pakoras.

qa.q: Why did Kishore go back inside from the stairwell?
qa.a: Kishore's anger was high and Kishore feared saying something ugly.

qa.q: What specific fix did Kishore propose?
qa.a: To play before nine or put a mat under the drum.

qa.q: How did the neighbour respond to the request?
qa.a: He blinked, then laughed, and put a folded blanket under the drum that same evening.

grounding: An elder recalls building irritation at a neighbour's noise, speaking calmly before it exploded and proposing a specific fix.

passage:
Rain was hammering the parking bay at 8:40, and Ramesh's interview across town was at 9:30. Once again, Kiran's hatchback sat sideways across his scooter's slot, the fourth time this month. Ramesh felt heat rise up his neck. He had already rehearsed a speech full of words he would regret.
Instead he rang the bell of 3B, dripping. Kiran opened, toothbrush in mouth.
"Sorry to disturb you. Your car's across my slot again, and I've an interview at nine-thirty. Could you move it now?"
Kiran winced and grabbed the keys.
As the car reversed, Ramesh leaned in at the window. "Can we fix this for good? If you park nose-in against the pillar, both fit. I've measured."
"Deal," Kiran said. "My bad."
Ramesh rode off, wet but calm. If it happened again, he'd raise it at the society meeting.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when he saw the car across his slot again?
qa.a: He felt angry and frustrated after it happened four times this month, with heat rising up his neck and a harsh speech ready in his head.

qa.q: What specific fix did Ramesh propose?
qa.a: That Kiran park nose-in against the pillar so both vehicles fit, which Ramesh had already measured.

qa.q: How might Kiran see the moment at the door?
qa.a: Kiran is caught off guard and a little embarrassed, but Ramesh's calm tone makes it easy to apologise and agree to the fix.

grounding: The protagonist's irritation at a neighbour's parking has built up; he speaks calmly, proposes a specific fix, and keeps society rules as a later step.

passage:
For two weeks, the black garbage bags from the flat opposite had been left on the landing overnight, and by morning the stray cats had torn them open. Yogesh stepped over eggshells on his way to work and felt his jaw clench every time.
On Sunday, before his anger could turn into a note taped to the door, he knocked. Harsha answered, looking tired, a baby on one hip.
"Hi, I'm Yogesh from 402. The bags on the landing are getting torn open by cats overnight. It's making a mess on the stairs."
"Oh no. The collector comes at seven and I'm up all night with this one," Harsha said.
"What if we share a covered bin by the stairs? I'll buy one this week. You put the bag in at night, it's safe till seven."
Harsha smiled. "That would really help."
Yogesh had checked the society rules on landings, just in case. He didn't need them.

qa.q: Who tore open the garbage bags on the landing?
What might Yogesh have been worried would happen if he waited longer?
qa.a: He was worried his irritation would turn into an angry note taped to the door, since his jaw clenched every time he stepped over the mess.

qa.q: Which choice solved the problem, and why?
qa.a: Proposing a shared covered bin by the stairs; it gave Harsha a way to leave the bag safely until the seven o'clock collection.

qa.q: Why might Harsha have left the bags out in the first place?
qa.a: Harsha seems exhausted, up all night with a baby, and probably relieved that Yogesh came with a solution rather than a complaint.

grounding: The protagonist's annoyance about a neighbour's garbage has built up; he speaks calmly, proposes a specific fix, and keeps the society rules in reserve.
